title: The High-Pressure Patient

history.hpc: Mr Krishnamurthy is attending for a routine IOP check as part of his glaucoma monitoring. He is on latanoprost eye drops once a night for both eyes. He says he has been using them every night as instructed. When the PSA informs him that the reading today is 26 mmHg in his right eye, Mr Krishnamurthy becomes alarmed: 'That is very high! Am I going blind? What does this number mean? Should I put more drops?' The PSA must complete the test correctly and manage the patient's concern appropriately.
history.pmhx: Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) diagnosed 3 years ago. Controlled hypertension. No diabetes.
medications: Latanoprost 0.005% eye drops OD nocte (both eyes)
history.social_hx: Bus driver. Worried about his driving license if his vision is affected.

iop.right: 26 mmHg — average of three NCT readings (25, 26, 27)
iop.left: 18 mmHg — average of three NCT readings (17, 18, 19)

examination_findings.fundus: Not assessed at this stage — doctor to review

nct.notes: Three readings taken per eye. Patient blinked on first attempt RE — reading discarded and repeated.

diagnosis: NCT completed. RE IOP elevated at 26 mmHg. LE IOP within normal range at 18 mmHg. PSA role is to document and report to doctor — not to interpret clinical significance or advise patient on medication changes.

immediate: Explain the NCT procedure: 'I will measure the pressure in your eye using a gentle puff of air — there is no needle or touching the eye.'
Position patient correctly at the slit lamp chinrest: forehead touching the rest, eyes open and looking at the fixation light
Take three readings per eye and average them
Discard and repeat any reading where the patient blinked or moved
Record all readings clearly on the clinic form

When patient asks about the reading, respond calmly: 'I understand you are worried. The doctor will review these numbers and explain what they mean for you. My job is to measure and record — the doctor is the right person to explain the results.'
Do NOT tell the patient his readings are 'high' or 'normal' — do NOT advise him to change his drops
If patient is distressed, acknowledge the feeling: 'It is understandable to feel anxious — the doctor will go through everything with you.'
follow_up: Hand completed IOP form to nurse and flag that the patient has questions for the doctor
Reassure patient he will be seen shortly
patient_education: Remind patient that IOP measurements are just one piece of information and the doctor will review everything
Advise patient to ask the doctor his questions directly — write them down if needed so he does not forget
Do not answer clinical questions about whether his glaucoma is worsening

key_points: Confirms patient identity (full name and NRIC or date of birth)
Notes the purpose of visit (glaucoma follow-up, IOP check)
Checks that patient is wearing no contact lenses before NCT
Acknowledges the patient's anxiety without giving clinical interpretation
Correctly positions patient at NCT: forehead rest, eyes open, looking at fixation light
Takes three readings per eye and uses the average
Discards and repeats readings where patient blinked or moved
Records all individual readings and the average clearly on the form
Does not interpret the IOP reading for the patient (does not say 'your pressure is high')
Does not advise medication changes under any circumstances
Correctly defers clinical interpretation to the doctor
Identifies the patient's distress and manages it with empathy, not clinical information
Handles the anxious patient calmly and with empathy
Refers clinical questions to the doctor — does not attempt to answer them
Documents all readings accurately and flags patient's concerns to clinical staff
Does not reveal or comment on the numerical IOP result beyond 'the doctor will review it'
